item.title: “And what, Mahānāma, is the gratification of sensual pleasures? Mahānāma, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure: forms cognizable by the eye – desirable,…
item.description:
“And what, Mahānāma, is the gratification of sensual pleasures? Mahānāma, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure: forms cognizable by the eye – desirable, pleasurable, agreeable, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing; sounds cognizable by the ear … odors cognizable by the nose … tastes cognizable by the tongue … tangibles cognizable by the body – desirable, pleasurable, agreeable, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. These, Mahānāma, are the five strands of sensual pleasure. The pleasure and joy that arise in dependence on these five strands of sensual pleasure – that is the gratification of sensual pleasures.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 14 – Cūḷadukkhakkhandhasutta

item.title: “Monks, devas and humans delight in form, are excited by form. When form changes, fades, and ceases, devas and humans dwell in suffering. Devas and…
item.description:
“Monks, devas and humans delight in form, are excited by form. When form changes, fades, and ceases, devas and humans dwell in suffering. Devas and humans delight in sound … in odor … in taste … in touch … in phenomena, are excited by phenomena. When phenomena change, fade, and cease, devas and humans dwell in suffering.

Forms, sounds, tastes, odors, touches,
And all phenomena —
Desirable, delightful, agreeable —
Thus they are called.

Devas and humans in the world,
Regarding them as delightful —
Where they cease and fade away,
Devas and humans see suffering.

The noble one sees as ease
When identity view is destroyed —
The noble one sees as opposite
All the views of the world.

What others call pleasure,
The noble call suffering.
What others call suffering,
The noble know as pleasure.

See the Dhamma, hard to comprehend,
Where the ignorant are bewildered —
Darkness for the blind,
Obscurity for those who cannot see.

The wise are open-eyed,
Like light clearly shining,
The foolish, even though near,
Do not understand the Dhamma.

Overcome by the thirst of birth,
Swept away by the current of existence,
Subject to Māra’s control —
They do not awaken to this Dhamma.

Apart from the noble ones, no one
Awakens to this path —
The path leading to Nibbāna,
With perfect wisdom, free from defilements.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.136

item.title: Elder Nun Mother of Vaḍḍha: Vaḍḍha, never fall into the realm of sensual desire. My son, do not share In repeated suffering. Blissful is the…
item.description:
Elder Nun Mother of Vaḍḍha:

Vaḍḍha, never fall into the realm of sensual desire.
My son, do not share
In repeated suffering.

Blissful is the sage,
Without desire, with doubt cut off,
Cooled, self-controlled,
Without any defilements.

That sage practices
The path leading to right view,
Putting an end to suffering.
Vaḍḍha, strive on!

With confidence, mother spoke
This purpose for you —
“My dear mother! I think
That you have no sensual desire.”

“Vaḍḍha, whatever conduct —
Low, high, or middling —
Not even a little sensual desire
Exists in me.

I have destroyed all defilements,
Not heedless, meditating.
The three true knowledges are attained —
The Buddha’s instruction is done.”

Wonderful, my mother,
Encouraging and urging me,
With verses of truth,
Out of compassion.

Hearing my mother’s words,
Her motherly instruction,
I practiced the Dhamma gratefully,
Attaining security from bondage.

I am energetic, striving,
Day and night not lazy.
Well encouraged by my mother,
I attained the supreme purity.

From: Therīgāthā 9.1

item.title: “Monks, suppose there is urine mixed with various medicines. Then a person with jaundice comes, and someone says to him: ‘Good man, this urine is…
item.description:
“Monks, suppose there is urine mixed with various medicines. Then a person with jaundice comes, and someone says to him: ‘Good man, this urine is mixed with various medicines. If you wish, drink it. While drinking, you will not delight in its color, smell, or taste. But after drinking, you will be at ease.’ That person might drink it after reflection, without refusal. While drinking, he does not delight in its color, smell, or taste. But after drinking, he is at ease. Monks, I say that this course of practice is like that simile — namely, a course of practice that is painful in the present but has pleasant results in the future.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 46 – Mahādhammasamādānasutta

item.title: “Monks, there are these five dangers for one who is mindless, not clearly comprehending, and falls asleep. What five? He sleeps badly; he wakes up…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these five dangers for one who is mindless, not clearly comprehending, and falls asleep. What five? He sleeps badly; he wakes up badly; he has bad dreams; devas do not protect him; impure things flow out, nocturnal emission. These, monks, are the five dangers for one who is mindless, not clearly comprehending, and falls asleep. Monks, there are these five benefits for one who is mindful, clearly comprehending, and falls asleep. What five? He sleeps well; he wakes up well; he has no bad dreams; devas protect him; impure things do not flow out. These, monks, are the five benefits for one who is mindful, clearly comprehending, and falls asleep.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.210

item.title: “And how, monks, does a monk dwell ‘as below, so above; as above, so below’? Here, monks, a monk contemplates this body from the soles…
item.description:
“And how, monks, does a monk dwell ‘as below, so above; as above, so below’? Here, monks, a monk contemplates this body from the soles of the feet upward, from the top of the head downward, enclosed by skin and full of various impurities: ‘There are in this body: head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, intestinal mesentery, stomach, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, skin oil, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine.’ Thus, monks, a monk dwells ‘as below, so above; as above, so below.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 51.20

item.title: “One who does not go too far, Nor lag behind, Having overcome all this unreality — That monk abandons the near and far shore, Like…
item.description:
“One who does not go too far,
Nor lag behind,
Having overcome all this unreality —
That monk abandons the near and far shore,
Like a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.”

“One who does not go too far,
Nor lag behind,
Knowing that all this is unreality —
That monk abandons the near and far shore,
Like a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.”

“One who does not go too far,
Nor lag behind,
Free from greed, free from hatred,
Free from delusion —
That monk abandons the near and far shore,
Like a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.”

From: Sutta Nipāta 1.1

item.title: “‘For life, the arahants have abandoned unchastity, live the holy life, live secluded, abstaining from sexual intercourse, the low practice. Today, this night and day,…
item.description:
“‘For life, the arahants have abandoned unchastity, live the holy life, live secluded, abstaining from sexual intercourse, the low practice. Today, this night and day, I too abandon unchastity, live the holy life, live secluded, abstaining from sexual intercourse, the low practice. In this factor, I follow the arahants and will observe the uposatha day.’ This is the third factor attained.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.18

item.title: “Monks, while Prince Vipassī was going to the pleasure garden, he saw a sick person, suffering, gravely ill, wallowing in his own urine and feces,…
item.description:
“Monks, while Prince Vipassī was going to the pleasure garden, he saw a sick person, suffering, gravely ill, wallowing in his own urine and feces, needing others to lift him, needing others to support him. Seeing this, the prince asked the charioteer: ‘Good man, what has this person done that his eyes are not like those of others, his voice not like others?’ ‘Your Highness, that is called a sick person.’ ‘Good man, why is he called a sick person?’ ‘Your Highness, he is called a sick person because he has not recovered from his illness.’ ‘Good man, then am I subject to sickness, not having fallen sick yet?’ ‘Your Highness, you and I as well — all of us are subject to sickness, even though we have not fallen sick yet.’ ‘Good man, then this visit to the pleasure garden is enough. Drive back to the palace.’ ‘Yes, Your Highness.’ Monks, the charioteer, obeying the prince, drove back to the palace. Monks, Prince Vipassī returned to the palace, suffering, grieving, and thought: ‘Shameful indeed is this birth! And anyone who is born must also age, must also be sick!’”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 14 – Mahāpadānasutta

item.title: “Monks, form is suffering, both in the past and in the future, not to mention the present. Seeing this, monks, a well-taught noble disciple has…
item.description:
“Monks, form is suffering, both in the past and in the future, not to mention the present. Seeing this, monks, a well-taught noble disciple has no regret for past form, does not delight in future form, and practices disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present form. Feeling is suffering … Perception is suffering … Formations are suffering … Consciousness is suffering, both in the past and in the future, not to mention the present. Seeing this, monks, a well-taught noble disciple has no regret for past consciousness, does not delight in future consciousness, and practices disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation regarding present consciousness.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.10
